title: Readiness Is a Reserve You Spend
hook: A carrier's record 266-day deployment isn't a story about a weak military. It's a story about a budget nobody tracks: the finite reserve of crew rest and maintenance that every deployment draws down.
key_points: The USS Abraham Lincoln deployed for 266 days, about 200 of them in a combat zone — crew on minimal sleep, with documented mental strain.
Monica Duffy Toft's argument: readiness is a finite reserve that gets spent whether or not the war was necessary.
Operational tempo means the pace and duration units operate, plus the recovery time they get — high tempo cancels the recovery.
Extended operations consume scheduled maintenance windows, degrade equipment, and drive people out through burnout and broken relationships.
Interventions rose from just over 2.3 a year in the Cold War to 3.48 annually after 1991 — roughly a 50% increase; 1974 was the last year with none.
The 2017 precedent: 37% of warfare readiness certifications for cruiser and destroyer crews in Japan had expired; the Fitzgerald and McCain collisions killed 17 sailors.
content_html: When the USS Abraham Lincoln came home after 266 days at sea — roughly 200 of them in a combat zone — the headline looked like a story about a strained military. Monica Duffy Toft, who directs the Center for Strategic Studies at Tufts' Fletcher School, reads it differently: the strain is real, but it traces back to civilian choices about how often to use the force, not to a military that has gotten weak.
extra_html:
The idea at the center of her argument is that readiness is a finite reserve. A ship or a unit is only ready because it has been through a cycle: deploy, come back, do deferred maintenance, let people sleep and see their families, recertify skills. Push the deployment longer and you don't just tire people out — you spend the maintenance window, the equipment life, and the retention you were going to need next year. Toft's phrase for it is that the reserve "gets spent whether or not the war was necessary." The technical term for the throttle is operational tempo: the pace and duration at which units operate and the recovery time they actually receive. Raise the tempo and the recovery half of the cycle is what gets cut first.

Her comparative claim is that the demand side has grown while the danger has not tracked it. Writing in The Conversation, she notes the U.S. averaged just over 2.3 new military interventions a year during the Cold War, rising to 3.48 annually after 1991 — about a 50% increase — and that 1974 was the last year the country launched none. The Army stretched Iraq-era tours to 15 months; the Navy has its own cautionary case, when by June 2017 some 37% of warfare readiness certifications for cruiser and destroyer crews based in Japan had expired, the same year collisions involving the USS Fitzgerald and the USS John S. McCain killed 17 sailors. The lesson she draws is that readiness debates that focus only on budgets and ship counts miss the part that can't be appropriated: time to recover. (This card describes the U.S. case specifically, and reflects the author's argument.)

related.hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

related.title: The 60-Day Clock That Keeps Getting Reset
related.hook: The War Powers Resolution gives Congress 60 days to approve a war before the president must stop — but a new 'notice' can restart the clock, and Congress has struggled to make its objection stick.

related.title: Why Ceasefires Break Down
related.hook: A ceasefire stops the shooting. It does not make peace. The difference — and the danger — lies in everything a quick deal leaves out.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean to call military readiness a 'finite reserve'?
flashcards.back_html: Readiness is a stock, not a switch: every deployment draws down crew rest, maintenance windows, and equipment life — and it gets spent whether or not the war was necessary.

flashcards.prompt: What is operational tempo, as the article defines it?

choices.text: The pace and duration at which units operate, plus the recovery time they receive
The total number of ships and aircraft a service owns
The share of the defense budget spent on new equipment

flashcards.explanation_html: Tempo is about rhythm, not size. When deployments get extended, the recovery half of the cycle disappears and strain cascades.

flashcards.prompt: Toft argues the U.S. military is overstretched relative to what?

choices.text: The wars its civilian leadership chooses to fight, not the actual level of danger
The size of the militaries it might have to face
The number of allies it has treaty obligations to defend

flashcards.explanation_html: Her point is that the strain traces to civilian decisions about how often to intervene — intervention rates rose about 50% after 1991 — rather than to a rising threat.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the Navy's 2017 experience a warning about high tempo?
flashcards.back_html: By June 2017, 37% of warfare readiness certifications for cruiser and destroyer crews in Japan had expired — and the Fitzgerald and McCain collisions that year killed 17 sailors.
